why: This is the church that sang its teaching rather than argued it in treatises - Ephrem's hymns carried its doctrine, and men and women bound themselves to a covenant of celibacy and service inside the ordinary congregation, not apart from it.
sourcing: Rich in hymns and doctrinal teaching (Ephrem, Aphrahat's twenty-three Demonstrations); thin on ordinary believers, the daughters of the covenant's own words, and the years after Ephrem's death in 373.
floorNote: This tradition holds the doctrine the Nicene Creed states. One figure inside it, the philosopher-poet Bardaisan, taught cosmological ideas his own later tradition repudiated; exactly where he stands relative to that doctrine remains an open question.
relationsSummary: Its see of Nisibis passed into the Church of the East. The Syriac Orthodox Church also counts it as a root. Syriac translators later carried Greek philosophy and medicine into Arabic. From there, that learning came back to Europe.
voices: Ephrem was a deacon, first at Nisibis and then, after 363, at Edessa, and this tradition's most prolific poet: hundreds of hymns carried its doctrine in verse a congregation could sing. He spent his last year running famine relief in the city and died within the month the crisis ended.

Aphrahat, remembered simply as 'the Persian sage,' wrote twenty-three dated letters from inside the Persian empire between 336 and 345, the last of them composed deep inside Shapur's persecution. He once drafted a circular letter in a synod of bishops' own name, yet whether he held that office himself is a question his own tradition never answers.

Tatian wove the four Gospels into one continuous story a generation before this Christian tradition's own window opens, and Edessa's later founding story pictures its people hearing his harmony read. Greek church history also remembers him breaking with Rome and founding a rigorist sect of his own—a controversy that belongs to his life outside this Syriac tradition, not inside it.

Bardaisan was a philosopher and poet at the court of King Abgar the Great. His one surviving dialogue argues that free will, not the stars, decides how people live—Christians the world over follow one law, whatever horoscope they were born under. His own later tradition rejected him over a separate question, whether the body itself is raised, and exactly where he stood on it is a question the record leaves open.

Jacob, bishop of Nisibis from about 309 and a signatory at the Council of Nicaea in 325, was remembered as the city's protector through Persian siege — though even his own people could not agree on when he died: the Chronicle of Edessa places it in 337 or 338, while Theodoret's history has him still at his post through a siege.

The daughters of the covenant were women vowed to God for life. Not one line composed by one of them survives; everything known of them, even the words Aphrahat gives one of them to say, was written by men.

Simeon bar Sabbae, bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, was ordered to collect a crushing new tax on Persia's Christians and refused. Arrested and brought before Shapur II, tradition says he was offered gifts, then threatened, and each time refused to worship the sun. He was executed with his own clergy — tradition remembers him as the first of the persecution's bishops to die for his faith. His death opened the twenty-year vacancy the Persian church endured.
legacy:
Syriac is still a language of worship in the Assyrian Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox Church, and the Eastern Catholic churches in union with Rome. All of them still sing Ephrem's hymns.

Within a generation of this tradition's own close, the Gospel harmony Edessa's later founding story pictures these communities reading gave way to a new translation, the Peshitta, and churches began reading the four Gospels separately again. Tradition credits Bishop Rabbula of Edessa (411–435) with the change.

Missionaries carried the faith east along the trade routes into Persia and India, and by the seventh century as far as Tang-dynasty China. Centuries later, Syriac translators became the channel through which Greek philosophy and medicine reached the Arabic-speaking world, and from there passed back into Europe.

A separate school of formal theological training later grew up at Nisibis—founded around 490, two generations after this tradition's own record closes—and became one of the ancient world's most important centers of Christian education, distinct from the teaching Jacob and Ephrem had given the same city a century earlier.

The name of the covenant lasted. The acts of the synod of 410 use it in the king's grant, and in the sixth century John of Ephesus still writes of women becoming "readers and daughters of the covenant." Edessa also kept the memory of Persia's martyrs: Sozomen says some sixteen thousand were known by name, with a multitude beyond counting, and that the people of Edessa took great care over their names.

uncertain: Whether Bishop Jacob lived through the siege. Theodoret, writing about a century later, says the Persians dammed the river Mygdonius and broke the walls with its water, that Jacob prayed inside the church while the walls were built up again, and that at Ephrem's request he climbed a tower and called down mosquitoes and gnats on the army; the wonders are his. Ephrem's own hymn on the bishops of Nisibis says the city's first priest was already "dead and buried within her," his body a wall for the city. The Chronicle of Edessa puts Jacob's death in the year 649 of the Greeks, 337 or 338.
The year of the siege. Ephrem's hymn calls it the city's "third peril" and gives no year.
The year of the flood. The Chronicle of Edessa sets it in November of the year 513 of the Greeks, which is 201. The translator's notes give 202, and say that Dionysius places the flood in 216.

Why the king turned on the Christians of Persia. Sozomen says the Magi were angered when the Christians grew in number, formed churches and appointed priests and deacons, and that the king believed a charge that their bishop was a friend of the Roman emperor. The Syriac acts of the Persian martyrs put the king's reason in his own mouth: that the bishop would make his people servants of the emperor, who shared their faith.

The one-story Gospel. Only Edessa's late founding story, the Doctrine of Addai, has these churches reading the Diatessaron, and no old line places it at Nisibis or across the whole period. The word itself is the St Petersburg manuscript's reading, which confirms the first editor's guess at an unclear word.

The covenant in 410. The synod's acts use the same word for those the king freed, but the editor of the acts reads it there as the whole clergy, monks included, so it is not shown to be the same vowed order Aphrahat wrote for.
Ephrem's birthplace. Sozomen says he was "a native of Nisibis, or his family was of the neighboring territory."

Why the later king changed course. The acts of 410 say his grant came about in the time of Mar Isaac, through the work of the bishop Marutha, the go-between of peace and concord between East and West, and of the bishops of the Romans. Socrates, a generation later, has the Roman emperor send Maruthas to the Persian king. No old line gives the king's own reason, and the acts do not say whether East and West mean the two empires or the two churches.
briefReferences: The Chronicle of Edessa, entry 8 (line 53): in November of the year 513 of the Greeks, after a great and violent rain in the night, the river broke down the western wall. King Abgar had stood on the tower called that of the Persians and watched the water by the light of torches. The flood overthrew his palace, destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians and killed more than two thousand, many of them asleep. Line 59: the city's scribes recorded it, and the archivists kept it. Entries 104-105 (lines 251-253): its last years, under Justinian.

Sozomen, Church History III.16 (lines 32053-32054): Ephrem learned in the language of the Syrians. Theodoret, Church History II.26 (lines 11065-11067): Nisibis on the borders of Persia and Rome. The Doctrine of Addai (line 65, with the editor's note, line 219): the people coming day by day to the readings of the Old and New Testament and of the Diatessaron. Eusebius, Church History IV.29 (lines 26368, 26424-26433, 26479): Tatian, a hearer of Justin, made the Diatessaron, "still in the hands of some." Tatian, Address to the Greeks (line 7460): born in the land of the Assyrians.

Aphrahat, Demonstration VI.1-4 (lines 25803-25808, 25835-25846): the vowed keep watch, sing psalms and pray, give their goods to the poor, and do not live with the other sex, lest lust draw them on. Parisot's Latin, Demonstration VII.21 (lines 21939-21942): the preachers warn the whole covenant before baptism; his introduction (lines 3291-3293): the Syriac name means sons of the covenant. Demonstration XXII.25 (lines 28517-28519, 28554-28561): written for the children of the Church of God, twenty-two letters for the twenty-two letters of the alphabet, the first ten in the year 648 of Alexander and the last twelve in 655, which the editor's note gives as 337 and 344.
Aphrahat, Demonstration VI.7 (Johnston's English, lines 25948-25953; Parisot's Latin, lines 18126-18134): the words he gives a daughter of the covenant to answer a vowed man.

Ephrem, Nisibene Hymn I (lines 13725-13734): Noah's flood, the bow and the refrain; lines 13746-13751: "mounds and weapons and waves encircle me," and the river threatens the city; lines 13839-13840: the city's "third peril." The collection's heading (lines 13710-13715): the siege of Nisibis.

Sozomen, Church History II.9 (lines 28873-28877, 28889-28899): the Magi angered, the charge against the bishop, the tax and its aim, the priests killed and the churches pulled down. Aphrahat, Demonstration XXI (lines 27416-27419): the reproach that vexed him, "If they have a God, why does He not avenge His people?"; lines 27988-27991: many confess and are slain; the year from lines 28558-28561.

Socrates, Church History III.22 (lines 11679-11697): the new emperor, his army in danger inside Persia, gives up Nisibis. Barhadbeshabba (lines 20435-20438): Ephrem withdraws to Edessa. Ephrem, Prose Refutations (lines 584, 431, 640, 606-608, 917, 1605-1609): Marcion's Stranger, Mani's two Roots and the Earth of Light, Bardaisan's five Entities in empty Space; line 1205: their fast like ours, their faith not like ours, and praying with Satan. Sozomen III.16 (lines 32085-32103): Bardaisan's son's songs and Ephrem's hymns in the same meters.

The Chronicle of Edessa, entry 30 (line 103): Ephrem dies on the ninth of June in the year 684 of the Greeks. Palladius, Lausiac History 40 (line 471): Ephrem, deacon of the Church of Edessa. Sozomen III.16 (lines 32101-32103): from then on the Syrians sang his hymns.

The Synod of Isaac (Chabot's French): in the king's eleventh year (line 16155), his grant rebuilding the churches, freeing the prisoners and letting the priests, the leaders and all the holy covenant go freely (lines 16159-16166); the grant coming about in the time of Mar Isaac (lines 16168-16169), through the work of the bishop Marutha, the go-between of peace and concord between East and West (lines 16227-16230), and of the bishops of the Romans (lines 16236-16237); the bishops gathered in the great church of the capital (lines 16410-16416); forty bishops, one bishop for each city and the feasts kept together (lines 16519-16534); the list of sees, Nisibis after Seleucia-Ctesiphon and Beit Lapat, and a city's two or three bishops not accepted (lines 17714-17742); Hosea of Nisibis, second metropolitan (line 17746) and third to sign (lines 17856-17861); the day like the dead rising (lines 16422, 16499-16500). Socrates, Church History VII.8 (lines 19135-19141, 19174-19176): the Roman emperor sends Maruthas, bishop of Mesopotamia, on a mission to the king of the Persians, who then lets him build churches wherever he wishes.

quotationOriginals.modern: I am promised in marriage to a royal husband, and I serve him. If I leave his service and serve you, my bridegroom will be angry with me. He will write me a letter of divorce and send me away from his house.
quotationOriginals.printed: To a royal husband am I betrothed, and Him do I serve; and if I leave His service and serve thee, my betrothed will be wroth with me, and will write me a letter of divorce, and will send me away from His house
quotationOriginals.work: Aphrahat, Demonstration VI (Of Monks), section 7, tr. A. E. Johnston (Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, 13)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Johnston's English. The Syriac is held only in unreadable scan text. Parisot's Latin of the Syriac (lines 18130-18134) confirms the reading, and its Sponsus meus gives "my bridegroom" for "my betrothed"; the scan runs three of its words together.
